title: What the first ten seconds of a startup homepage have to do
scene: A dim desk with an iMac showing a code editor beside a portfolio page, a second monitor with a mountain wallpaper, and a lit lamp.
angle: Judge those seconds by two questions only: what is this, and how do I talk to a person. A poetic brand line can stay if the next sentence answers both.

title: How to brief a studio for a marketing site
scene: A close view of a fountain pen writing on lined paper.
angle: A useful brief is short: who the site is for, the one action it should earn, three references you like, and what must not change. Skip the forty-page deck.

title: Landing page design for founders past the template
scene: A bright office window ledge with a laptop, a closed notebook, white chairs, and a tall indoor tree.
angle: Templates fail when the product is specific. Show how to keep a simple page while replacing generic sections with the founder's actual offer.

title: A pretty homepage versus a page that books calls
scene: A person gesturing in a meeting, with a laptop showing a colorful layout, a notebook, and a phone on the table.
angle: Separate taste from the path to a call. Name the few elements that create a booked intro: offer, proof, and one action.

title: When a one-page site is enough
scene: A bright office window ledge with a laptop, a closed notebook, white chairs, and a tall indoor tree.
angle: Give a clear rule: one page while there is one offer and one audience. Split when people arrive with different jobs, such as hiring, buying, and reading docs.

title: How to rewrite a homepage headline
scene: A close view of a fountain pen writing on lined paper.
angle: Walk through a rewrite method: say the audience, the outcome, and the contrast with the old way. Use before-and-after lines that are invented as exercises, clearly labeled as exercises, not as client work.

title: The pages a seed-stage site actually needs
scene: A hand pinning string between printed mobile screens on a wall.
angle: Recommend a small set: home, product or service, proof, about, and a way to start a conversation. Explain what to postpone.

title: What to put above the fold when the product is hard to explain
keyword: explain a complex product on a website
scene: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it.
angle: Use a concrete object, a one-sentence job, and a picture of the interface. Warn against leading with category jargon.

title: How a marketing site gets scoped so the date survives
scene: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops.
angle: Show a scope built from pages and states, not from vague phases. Include what a change request does to the date.

title: A checklist before you publish a company site
scene: Hands typing on a laptop at a wooden desk near a window.
angle: A practical pre-publish list: copy, links, forms, mobile, titles, alt text, speed, and the inbox that receives replies.

title: Signs a website needs a revamp
scene: A hand pinning string between printed mobile screens on a wall.
angle: List observable signs: the offer changed, the page is slow, editing is scary, mobile is an afterthought. Separate boredom with the design from a real need.

title: How to redesign without losing people who already trust you
scene: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals on a sheet of paper.
angle: Keep the name, the offer, and the paths regulars use. Change the structure only where it is failing. Mention Thomas Bewick as a heritage brand that needed a modern site without losing the craft.

title: What to keep in an ecommerce redesign
scene: A clothing shop interior with folded shirts, hanging jackets, shelves, and pendant lights.
angle: Keep catalog truth, urls that already rank, and the tone of the brand. Rebuild the parts shoppers feel: navigation, product pages, checkout. Down the Cove is the public example of leaving WooCommerce.

title: Migrating a store without a week of broken checkout
scene: An OPEN sign hanging in a shop window, with the word SHOP printed on the glass.
angle: Sequence: staging, catalog parity, payment in test, DNS last, a person watching the first real orders.

title: Frontend revamp or full rebuild
scene: A silver laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, with a monitor, mug, and phone behind it.
angle: A revamp when the content model and urls are sound. A rebuild when the stack cannot be edited safely or the offer has changed shape.

title: What clean code means on a marketing site
scene: A silver laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, with a monitor, mug, and phone behind it.
angle: Clean means a later editor can find the headline, the sections, and the images without a treasure hunt. Tie this to Hanabi's clean-code standard.

title: How to review a redesign before it ships
scene: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals on a sheet of paper.
angle: Review against the brief, not against personal taste. Give a pass for mobile, for the primary action, and for words a stranger understands.

title: A mobile-first redesign for desktop-first teams
scene: A close view of a smartphone home screen filled with app icons on a pale table.
angle: Start from the phone width the founder actually checks. Show what gets cut, what stacks, and what must remain tappable.

title: Replatforming a site without throwing away search equity
scene: Skyscrapers photographed from street level against a pale sky.
angle: Redirects, titles, and the same answers on the new urls. Do not promise rankings. Explain the work that protects them.

title: The handoff that makes a redesign usable after the studio leaves
scene: A person gesturing in a meeting, with a laptop showing a colorful layout, a notebook, and a phone on the table.
angle: Handoff is the repo, the content map, and a place the brand files live. The Hanabi portal is the concrete version: assets, docs, and updates.

title: Product design for founders who are also the first user
scene: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals on a sheet of paper.
angle: The founder's own use is evidence, not the whole spec. Show how to separate personal habit from the next user's job.

title: How to design an MVP that feels finished
scene: Two white smartwatch mockups on a plain light background, one showing the face and one the back.
angle: Finished means the narrow path is polished: empty, error, success, and the one workflow. Unfinished is a wide product with rough edges everywhere.

title: Fewer screens, a clearer product
scene: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it.
angle: Cut screens by merging steps that share a decision. Use a trading or lead tool as the kind of interface that gets worse when it shows everything. Got Next and Leadly are public examples of focused product UI.

title: Designing dashboards people can scan
scene: A silver laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, with a monitor, mug, and phone behind it.
angle: A scan is a hierarchy: what changed, what needs a decision, what can wait. Trade Moai is the public example of an interface organized around scanning.

title: Empty states, errors, and the screens teams forget
scene: A close view of a smartphone home screen filled with app icons on a pale table.
angle: Specify the blank screen, the first success, and the failure. Those three teach the product faster than the happy path.

title: How to run a design critique in a small team
scene: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops.
angle: A critique asks whether the work does the job. It is not a tour of preferences. Give a 30-minute shape a founder can host.

title: UX writing for teams that do not have a writer
scene: A close view of a fountain pen writing on lined paper.
angle: Buttons, errors, and empty states are the writing. Give a method: name the action, say what happens next, cut the mood.

title: Onboarding that respects a busy user's time
scene: Two people pointing at a laptop screen, one wearing a fitness band.
angle: Start with the user's job, not a product tour. Defer accounts and tutorials until the person has seen value.

title: When to prototype in Figma and when to design in the browser
scene: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it.
angle: Figma for structure and options. The browser when type, motion, and real content change the decision. Hanabi uses both Figma and production code.

title: Accessibility as a design quality bar
scene: A bright office window ledge with a laptop, a closed notebook, white chairs, and a tall indoor tree.
angle: Treat contrast, focus, names, and reduced motion as part of done. Point at WCAG as the reference, without pretending to certify a site.

title: Brand identity when you only have a name
scene: Blue and orange ink blooming through water.
angle: Start with audience, offer, and the feeling you refuse. A name is the seed. The system is type, color, and a sentence the site can repeat.

title: A logo is not a brand system
scene: Two white smartwatch mockups on a plain light background, one showing the face and one the back.
angle: The mark has to work small, on a dark surface, and next to type. The system is what keeps the next page from inventing a new palette.

title: A brand system small enough that a team will use it
scene: Hands typing on a laptop at a wooden desk near a window.
angle: A small system: one type pair, a short color list, logo files, and three sentences of voice. Large guideline books go unused.

title: Verbal identity: the sentences your site should sound like
scene: A close view of a fountain pen writing on lined paper.
angle: Pick three sentences the company is willing to say, and three it will not. Apply them to the homepage, the button, and the error.

title: Brand guidelines your engineers will actually open
scene: A silver laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, with a monitor, mug, and phone behind it.
angle: Engineers open a short page with files, hex values, and type settings. They do not open a mood film during a sprint.

title: What a client portal is for after the brand is delivered
scene: A long, quiet office corridor with glass rooms, a teal sofa, and a dark kitchen.
angle: A portal is where logos, tokens, docs, and project updates stay findable. Describe Hanabi's portal in those terms.

title: Naming a product without boxing the company in
scene: Skyscrapers photographed from street level against a pale sky.
angle: Test a name against the url, the sentence it has to sit in, and the future product it must not forbid.

title: Photography and illustration direction for a young brand
scene: Blue and orange ink blooming through water.
angle: Direction is a decision about subject, crop, and what you will not show. Wabisabi is a public example of a calm, tactile visual world.

title: How brand and interface should share one idea
scene: A person gesturing in a meeting, with a laptop showing a colorful layout, a notebook, and a phone on the table.
angle: One idea should survive from the homepage into the product. If the site is quiet and the app is loud, the brand is unfinished.

title: Rebranding without confusing the people who already buy
scene: An OPEN sign hanging in a shop window, with the word SHOP printed on the glass.
angle: Rebrand when the offer or the audience changed, not when the team is bored. Keep the path regulars use while the surface changes.

title: Why a marketing site should be fast before it is clever
scene: A silver laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, with a monitor, mug, and phone behind it.
angle: Clever motion on a slow page reads as carelessness. Argue for a fast first paint, then the one motion that explains something.

title: What founders should expect from a Next.js company site
scene: A dim desk with an iMac showing a code editor beside a portfolio page, a second monitor with a mountain wallpaper, and a lit lamp.
angle: Explain what the founder actually gets: a fast public site, a repo they own, and a place for content. Skip framework trivia.

title: Core Web Vitals in plain language
scene: A long, quiet office corridor with glass rooms, a teal sofa, and a dark kitchen.
angle: Explain LCP, INP, and CLS with the official thresholds and a plain example of each. This is the post that is allowed to be definitional.

title: Motion that helps, and motion that makes people leave
scene: A close view of a smartphone home screen filled with app icons on a pale table.
angle: Motion should show relationship or state. Looping decoration that fights reading should go. Tie this to Hanabi's reduced-motion standard.

title: Reduced motion is part of the craft
scene: A bright office window ledge with a laptop, a closed notebook, white chairs, and a tall indoor tree.
angle: Ship two versions of a move: the intended one, and a still or instant version when the person asks the system to reduce motion.

title: Why TypeScript matters on a public site
scene: A silver laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, with a monitor, mug, and phone behind it.
angle: The value is fewer broken props and safer edits, not a badge. Explain it as protection for the next person in the repo.

title: Choosing a CMS when the marketing team is small
keyword: cms for a small marketing team
scene: Hands typing on a laptop at a wooden desk near a window.
angle: Choose for who edits, how often, and whether drafts matter. Mention that Hanabi's own writing sits in Payload, separate from the client portal.

title: What you should own after a studio engagement
scene: Five people working on laptops around a wooden table.
angle: Own the repository, the domain, the analytics, and the content logins. A studio that keeps those is a dependency, not a partner.

title: Staging, DNS, and the week before launch
scene: A hand pinning string between printed mobile screens on a wall.
angle: The unglamorous sequence: a staging url, a content freeze, DNS with a rollback, and someone watching the first hour.

title: How to keep a site editable without a page-builder mess
scene: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it.
angle: Editors need structured fields for the things that change, not absolute freedom on every pixel. Explain the trade.

title: A design system for a team of five
scene: Hands typing on a laptop at a wooden desk near a window.
angle: A small system is type, color, space, and a handful of components. It is not a second product.

title: Tokens, type, and the decisions that stop visual drift
scene: Blue and orange ink blooming through water.
angle: A token is a named decision: the color, the size, the radius. Drift starts when people paste hex values into one-off screens.

title: Component libraries that match the brand
scene: Two white smartwatch mockups on a plain light background, one showing the face and one the back.
angle: Default component kits look like the kit. A useful library starts from the brand's type, color, and the few components the product repeats.

title: When a startup needs a design system
keyword: do startups need a design system
scene: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops.
angle: Need one when a second designer or a second product would otherwise invent a parallel style. Before that, a disciplined Figma file is enough.

title: Documenting components so the next engineer does not guess
scene: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it.
angle: Document the states and the don'ts. A picture of the happy path is not documentation.

title: Dark mode as a system decision
scene: A long, quiet office corridor with glass rooms, a teal sofa, and a dark kitchen.
angle: Dark mode is a second set of color decisions, planned with the first, not a filter added at the end.

title: Icons and illustration as part of the system
scene: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals on a sheet of paper.
angle: Pick a stroke, a grid, and a subject matter. Mixing three icon styles is how a product starts to look assembled from downloads.

title: How a brand kit stays alive after launch
scene: A person gesturing in a meeting, with a laptop showing a colorful layout, a notebook, and a phone on the table.
angle: Someone has to own changes. A portal or a short kit page beats a zip file in a chat thread.

title: Start AI automation with one boring workflow
scene: Two people pointing at a laptop screen, one wearing a fitness band.
angle: Pick a repeated chore with a clear input and output. Skip the platform that promises to automate the company.

title: What a Telegram bot is good for
scene: A close view of a smartphone home screen filled with app icons on a pale table.
angle: Good for a known group and a short list of commands: status, intake, alerts. Bad as a substitute for a product people have not asked to live inside a chat.

title: Discord bots as a product surface
scene: A person in a purple shirt typing on a bright blue laptop at a round table.
angle: A bot belongs where the community already talks. Design the commands as a small interface, with help text and a way to reach a human.

title: Designing an AI feature people can trust
scene: Two people pointing at a laptop screen, one wearing a fitness band.
angle: Trust comes from showing the source, the limit, and an easy edit. A confident wrong answer is a product defect.

title: When a service business should add automation
scene: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops.
angle: Automate the repeated handoff, not the judgment the client is paying for. A studio is the example: scheduling and file delivery, not the design critique.

title: Where a human still has to review the work
scene: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals on a sheet of paper.
angle: Review stays on anything a customer will see, pay, or be unable to undo. Draw the line explicitly.

title: Adding AI without turning the product into a chat box
scene: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it.
angle: Put the assist on the field or the draft the person was already editing. A blank chat is a new product they did not ask to learn.

title: How a studio can use AI in design without handing over judgment
scene: A person gesturing in a meeting, with a laptop showing a colorful layout, a notebook, and a phone on the table.
angle: AI can widen options and speed production chores. The studio still decides what is clear, what is on brand, and what ships.

title: Support automation that does not sound like a script
scene: A person in a purple shirt typing on a bright blue laptop at a round table.
angle: Use the brand's sentences. Offer a person when the question leaves the script. Do not pretend the bot is a named employee.

title: How to tell whether an automation saved time
scene: Hands typing on a laptop at a wooden desk near a window.
angle: Measure the minutes of the old chore against the minutes of review. If review takes longer, remove the automation.

title: Ecommerce design for a brand, not a marketplace
scene: A clothing shop interior with folded shirts, hanging jackets, shelves, and pendant lights.
angle: A brand shop is a edited room, not an infinite grid. Down the Cove and the calm of Wabisabi are the kinds of reference, without inventing their sales numbers.

title: Product pages that explain the thing, then step aside
scene: Two white smartwatch mockups on a plain light background, one showing the face and one the back.
angle: Lead with the object, the price, and the one reason it exists. Supporting detail comes after the decision is possible.

title: The checkout fields that cost the sale
scene: An OPEN sign hanging in a shop window, with the word SHOP printed on the glass.
angle: Use Baymard's published abandonment research carefully and cite it. Argue for fewer fields, visible cost, and a guest path when the brand allows it.

title: Mobile shopping for a brand with a point of view
scene: A close view of a smartphone home screen filled with app icons on a pale table.
angle: The phone page still has to feel like the brand. Crop, type, and the thumb's path matter more than a shrunk desktop grid.

title: What to migrate from WooCommerce, and what to leave
scene: A clothing shop interior with folded shirts, hanging jackets, shelves, and pendant lights.
angle: Bring products, customers you are allowed to contact, orders you must keep, and urls. Leave plugins that existed to patch the old theme.

title: Photography, crop, and the product grid
scene: Two white smartwatch mockups on a plain light background, one showing the face and one the back.
angle: Consistent crop and background do more for a grid than a new font. Show how mixed crops make a shop look unfinished.

title: The page and the email after purchase
scene: A bright office window ledge with a laptop, a closed notebook, white chairs, and a tall indoor tree.
angle: Confirmation should say what happens next, when it arrives, and how to ask a question. The email repeats that in plainer words.

title: Variants and inventory without a messy product page
scene: A clothing shop interior with folded shirts, hanging jackets, shelves, and pendant lights.
angle: Show the choice that changes the object. Hide the matrix. Say when something is unavailable without dumping the shopper on an error.

title: How to hire a design and development studio
scene: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops.
angle: Hire for the kind of work in the portfolio, the people who will actually do it, and whether you will own the result.

title: Studio, freelancer, or in-house for a first serious site
scene: Five people working on laptops around a wooden table.
angle: A freelancer for a narrow skill, in-house when the work never stops, a studio when you need design and build together for a defined launch.

title: What a good intro call should decide
scene: A person in a purple shirt typing on a bright blue laptop at a round table.
angle: The call should end with fit, a rough shape of the work, and whether a proposal is worth writing. It should not be a free strategy workshop.

title: Scoping a project when the idea is still loose
keyword: how to scope a website project
scene: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops.
angle: Name the unknown. Scope a first slice that will teach the rest, instead of pretending the whole product is known.

title: Communication habits that keep a build on track
scene: Five people working on laptops around a wooden table.
angle: A shared channel, a written decision, and a cadence. Hanabi's stated standard is clear updates, honest timelines, and fewer surprises.

title: Quality, clean code, flexibility, speed, and communication
scene: A person gesturing in a meeting, with a laptop showing a colorful layout, a notebook, and a phone on the table.
angle: Explain each of Hanabi's five differences as a behavior a client can see during a project, not as a slogan.

title: What to have ready before kickoff
scene: A hand pinning string between printed mobile screens on a wall.
angle: Accounts, a rough offer, access to the current site, and the name of the person who can approve. Missing access burns the first week.

title: How to give design feedback without restarting the project
scene: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals on a sheet of paper.
angle: React to the goal: clearer, more serious, easier to scan. Avoid redesigning in the margin unless the goal was wrong.

title: Fixed project or ongoing partnership
scene: A long, quiet office corridor with glass rooms, a teal sofa, and a dark kitchen.
angle: A fixed project for a launch with an edge. An ongoing partnership when the product keeps changing and you want the same people.

title: What a same-day response should mean
scene: A person in a purple shirt typing on a bright blue laptop at a round table.
angle: Same day means a human answer with the next step, not a finished design by dinner. Hanabi offers a same-day response by email.

title: How to read a studio portfolio
keyword: how to evaluate a design portfolio
scene: A dim desk with an iMac showing a code editor beside a portfolio page, a second monitor with a mountain wallpaper, and a lit lamp.
angle: Look for the problem, the restraint, and whether the studio built it. Screenshot galleries without a decision are decoration.

title: Questions to ask about performance, access, and ownership
keyword: questions to ask a web design agency
scene: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops.
angle: Ask who writes, who builds, what you will own, how motion treats reduced-motion users, and how the site stays fast.

title: Make the site search-ready before decorating it
scene: A dim desk with an iMac showing a code editor beside a portfolio page, a second monitor with a mountain wallpaper, and a lit lamp.
angle: Titles, headings, speed, and a sentence that says what the company is. Decoration on top of a vague page does not rank or convert.

title: Writing pages that AI search engines can cite
scene: A close view of a fountain pen writing on lined paper.
angle: Cite the Princeton GEO paper. Answer first, add a real source, and write a definition a model can lift. Do not stuff keywords.

title: FAQ sections that help buyers and search engines
scene: Hands typing on a laptop at a wooden desk near a window.
angle: Write questions buyers actually ask. Keep the answers visible. Point at FAQ schema only when the questions are on the page.

title: Internal linking for a small site
scene: A hand pinning string between printed mobile screens on a wall.
angle: Link from a specific sentence to the next useful page. A footer dump of every url helps less than a few honest links.

title: Titles and descriptions that earn the click
scene: A close view of a fountain pen writing on lined paper.
angle: The title is a promise the page keeps. Use Google's guidance on title links. Stay near 60 characters when you can.

title: Case-study pages that do more than show screenshots
keyword: how to write a design case study
scene: A person gesturing in a meeting, with a laptop showing a colorful layout, a notebook, and a phone on the table.
angle: A case study names the constraint, the decision, and what changed in the work. Screenshots illustrate that. They are not the whole piece.

title: Schema markup for a company site, in plain language
scene: A silver laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, with a monitor, mug, and phone behind it.
angle: Organization for the studio, FAQ only when visible, Article for posts. Schema does not replace clear writing.

title: Planning a blog that supports a product
scene: A bright office window ledge with a laptop, a closed notebook, white chairs, and a tall indoor tree.
angle: Each post should answer a search a buyer has and point at the product or the service. A disconnected magazine does not.

title: Niche positioning on a small site
scene: Skyscrapers photographed from street level against a pale sky.
angle: Say who it is for in the title and the first screen. A small studio ranks for a specific offer faster than for 'we do everything'.

title: Measure calls booked, not vanity traffic
scene: Hands typing on a laptop at a wooden desk near a window.
angle: The number that matters is the intro call or the email from the right kind of buyer. Sessions are context.

title: The first 90 days after a site launches
keyword: what to do after website launch
scene: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops.
angle: Watch queries, fix the lines people misunderstand, and publish into the gaps. Do not redesign again out of nerves.

title: A founder's map from brand to site to product
scene: Blue and orange ink blooming through water.
angle: The sequence Hanabi actually sells: a clear identity, a site that explains it, and an interface that behaves like the same idea.
